query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In this high‐entropy alloy, superconductivity emerges at low temperature because the high configurational entropy induces local lattice distortions that enhance the electron–phonon coupling. These distortions promote a conventional s‐wave pairing state in the dirty limit, so that despite the strong chemical disorder, the alloy exhibits a robust, well‐defined superconducting transition.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy synthesized in an as-cast state with an equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) composition of multiple transition metals arranged randomly on a simple lattice.
generation.intervention: Create a controlled variant of the alloy in which the configurational entropy is reduced—for example, by replacing one or more of the constituent metals with a dominant element (or by heat treatment to induce partial chemical ordering).
generation.conditions: Measurements to be made at low temperatures (below ~10 K) under identical ambient pressure and magnetic field conditions for both the original and modified alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and homogeneous chemical disorder arising from the high configurational entropy that modulate the electron–phonon interaction.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy leads to a random but homogeneous distribution of atomic sizes and bonding environments that cause subtle local distortions. These distortions enhance the electron–phonon coupling necessary for Cooper pair formation, while the s-wave symmetry (protected by Anderson’s theorem in the dirty limit) allows superconductivity to thrive despite the disorder. Reducing the mixing entropy is expected to lessen these beneficial distortions, thereby weakening the electron–phonon coupling and lowering the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as-synthesized high-entropy alloy will display a sharper transition to zero resistance at a higher Tc compared to the variant with reduced configurational entropy, which is expected to show a lower Tc and a broader superconducting transition.
generation.baseline: A chemically similar alloy with reduced configurational entropy (either by dominant element substitution or by inducing chemical ordering) should serve as a baseline showing weaker or absent superconductivity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in high-entropy alloys with moderate electron localization and conventional s-wave pairing; it may not apply if the disorder becomes so extreme that it localizes carriers or if magnetic impurities (or other pair-breaking effects) are introduced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect of entropy-induced lattice distortions on Tc and the precise balance between disorder-induced scattering and electron–phonon interaction remain uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the maximum configurational entropy (fully equiatomic high-entropy alloy) and one with reduced entropy (by replacing one or more elements to reduce the disorder or by applying a heat treatment to promote chemical ordering). Cool both samples under identical conditions while monitoring resistivity and magnetic susceptibility as temperature is lowered, alongside measuring critical current densities.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via resistivity (zero-resistance onset)
Magnetic susceptibility to detect the Meissner effect
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduction in configurational entropy does not lead to a measurable decrease in Tc or a notable broadening of the superconducting transition relative to the high-entropy sample, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy–induced lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon coupling (and consequently superconductivity) would be falsified.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. Robustness of superconductivity to external pressure in high-entropy-alloy-type metal telluride AgInSnPbBiTe5

Abstract: High-entropy-alloy (HEA) superconductors are a new class of disordered superconductors. However, commonality of superconducting characteristics of HEA materials is unclear. Here, we have investigated the crystal and electronic structure, and the robustness of superconducting states in a HEA-type metal telluride (MTe; M = Ag, In, Sn, Pb, Bi) under high pressure, and the results were compared with the pressure effects for a middle-entropy system (AgPbBiTe3) and a reference system of PbTe. When the crystal structure is CsCl-type, all phases show superconductivity under high pressure but exhibit different pressure dependences of the transition temperature (Tc). For PbTe, its Tc decreases with pressure. In contrast, the Tc of HEA-type AgInSnPbBiTe5 is almost independent of pressure, for pressures ranging from 13.0 to 35.1 GPa. Those results suggest that the robustness of superconductivity to external pressure is linked to the configurational entropy of mixing at the M site in MTe. Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEA) form through the random arrangement of five or more chemical elements on a crystalline lattice. Despite the significant amount of resulting compositional disorder, a subset of HEAs enters a superconducting state below critical temperatures, Tc<10 K. The superconducting properties of the known HEAs seem to suffice a Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) description, but little is known about their superconducting order parameter and the microscopic role of disorder. We report on magnetic susceptibility measurements on films of the superconducting HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x for characterizing the lower and upper critical fields Hc,1(T) and Hc,2(T), respectively as a function of temperature T. Our resulting analysis of the Ginzburg–Landau coherence length and penetration depth demonstrates that HEAs of this type are single-band isotropic s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit. Despite a significant difference in the elemental composition between the x=0.35 and x=0.71 films, we find that the observed Tc variations cannot be explained by disorder effects.Subject terms: Condensed-
